metadata.title: HPSC FSO Unit 3 Part B — 100 MCQs
metadata.source_scope: Uploaded 93-page HPSC Food Safety Officer Master Handout — Unit 3, Part B
metadata.exam_orientation: HPSC Food Safety Officer Group-B, 2026 recruitment cycle
metadata.answer_format: Questions and options first; consolidated answer_key second; detailed_explanations last.
metadata.pattern_note: The publicly reported revised HPSC scheme dated 16 October 2026 separates the objective Screening Test (General Studies/Haryana GK) from the subjective 150-mark Subject Knowledge Test. This technical MCQ bank is a revision and concept-checking resource, not a claim that the technical SKT is an MCQ paper.
metadata.regulatory_cutoff_note: Fortification-law questions are limited to the uploaded Fortification of Foods Regulations compendium, Version III dated 30 September 2021, including amendments reproduced there. This is not verification of all law presently in force.
metadata.source_gap_note: The uploaded documents do not establish the governing instrument or exact boundary wording for the requested 15%/25% Total Polar Compounds frying-oil thresholds or general 100/200 mg/kg food-colour limits. These are not asserted as verified legal limits.
metadata.prediction_caveat: Questions model technical FSO-style factual, conceptual, comparison, mechanism and regulatory-exception testing. No question can be guaranteed to appear.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Glycerol esterified with three fatty acids
detailed_explanations.explanation: A triacylglycerol is formed when the three hydroxyl groups of glycerol are esterified with fatty acids. The three chains may be identical or different. It is a major storage lipid and is classified as a simple lipid.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Glycerophospholipid
detailed_explanations.explanation: Compound lipids contain an additional group associated with the lipid framework. Glycerophospholipids contain a phosphate-bearing polar head group. Squalene, cholesterol and free fatty acids are treated as derived lipid constituents in the handout.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Sphingomyelin is a sphingolipid that also contains phosphate
detailed_explanations.explanation: Sphingolipids are built on a sphingoid-base framework rather than necessarily on glycerol. Sphingomyelin is a phosphorous-containing sphingolipid, while glycosphingolipids are both sphingolipids and glycolipids. The labels can overlap.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: 18 carbon atoms and two double bonds
detailed_explanations.explanation: In shorthand fatty-acid notation, the first number gives the total carbon atoms and the second gives the number of carbon–carbon double bonds. C18:2 alone does not reveal double-bond positions or cis/trans geometry.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Linoleic and alpha-linolenic acids
detailed_explanations.explanation: Linoleic acid (C18:2, omega-6) and alpha-linolenic acid (C18:3, omega-3) are essential fatty acids. Oleic acid is an omega-9 monounsaturated fatty acid; palmitic, stearic, butyric, lauric and capric acids are saturated.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: First double bond counted from the terminal methyl end
detailed_explanations.explanation: Omega notation counts from the terminal methyl (omega) end and identifies the position of the first double bond encountered. It does not state the total number of double bonds.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Butyric acid
detailed_explanations.explanation: Butyric acid is a short-chain fatty acid characteristic of milk fat. Milk fat also contains caproic, caprylic and capric acids, alongside major long-chain constituents such as palmitic, stearic and oleic acids.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Lauric acid
detailed_explanations.explanation: The handout describes lauric fats as containing approximately 40–50% lauric acid in the textbook account. Coconut and palm-kernel fats are examples. Palm oil and palm-kernel oil are chemically distinct and should not be confused.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Beta-sitosterol
detailed_explanations.explanation: Beta-sitosterol is a predominant phytosterol in many vegetable oils. Cholesterol predominates in animal fats. Squalene is a triterpene hydrocarbon, not a sterol.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Possible vegetable-fat addition to animal fat
detailed_explanations.explanation: Cholesterol acetate is reported at about 114°C, while phytosterol acetates are reported around 126–137°C. A higher-melting phytosterol-containing fraction can indicate vegetable-fat addition to animal fat, but mixtures and purification affect interpretation; it is not infallible.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: ROO• + RH → ROOH + R•
detailed_explanations.explanation: During propagation, a lipid radical reacts with oxygen to form a peroxyl radical (ROO•). The peroxyl radical abstracts hydrogen from another lipid (RH), producing a hydroperoxide (ROOH) and a new lipid radical. This sustains the chain reaction.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Hydroperoxides may decompose faster than they are formed
detailed_explanations.explanation: Peroxide value is a primary-oxidation index. At high temperatures, hydroperoxides are unstable and decompose into aldehydes, ketones, acids and other secondary products. A low value can therefore reflect advanced deterioration rather than freshness.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Free fatty acids and partial glycerides
detailed_explanations.explanation: Water cleaves ester bonds sequentially, yielding diacylglycerols, monoacylglycerols, free fatty acids and ultimately glycerol. Increased free fatty acids raise acidity and can lower the smoke point.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Decarboxylation of beta-keto acids formed in microbial metabolism
detailed_explanations.explanation: The handout explains ketonic rancidity as a microbial pathway in which certain fungi convert fatty acids through incomplete beta-oxidative routes to beta-keto acids. Decarboxylation produces methyl ketones. Controlled methyl-ketone formation can contribute to blue-cheese flavour.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Milligrams of KOH required per gram of fat
detailed_explanations.explanation: Saponification value is the milligrams of potassium hydroxide required to saponify one gram of fat under prescribed conditions. It reflects alkali demand for ester hydrolysis and is generally higher for fats with lower average fatty-acid chain length.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Greater unsaturation-related halogen uptake
detailed_explanations.explanation: Iodine value measures halogen uptake associated with carbon–carbon double bonds and is expressed as grams of iodine equivalent absorbed by 100 g fat. A higher value generally indicates greater unsaturation, but it does not identify omega family or every isomer.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Reichert–Meissl value
detailed_explanations.explanation: The Reichert–Meissl (RM) value operationally measures steam-volatile, water-soluble fatty acids, with butyric and caproic acids as important teaching associations. Polenske value concerns the steam-volatile, water-insoluble fraction.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Coconut or palm-kernel fat
detailed_explanations.explanation: Polenske value reflects steam-volatile, water-insoluble fatty acids, particularly caprylic and capric acids. It is useful in considering lauric-fat addition, especially coconut or palm-kernel fats. Plain palm oil should not be substituted for palm-kernel oil.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Acid value measures free acids; saponification value includes alkali consumed in ester hydrolysis
detailed_explanations.explanation: Acid value is the milligrams of KOH needed to neutralise free acids in one gram of sample. Saponification value measures alkali required to saponify the fat, including ester-bond hydrolysis. They answer different analytical questions.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Hydrolysis, thermal oxidation and polymerisation
detailed_explanations.explanation: Food-derived water promotes hydrolysis; oxygen and heat promote thermal oxidation; radical coupling and reactions of unsaturated chains produce dimers, trimers and polymers. These processes occur together during frying.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Strip some volatile compounds from the oil
detailed_explanations.explanation: Water leaving food as steam can strip some volatile oxidation products and agitate the oil. This may help volatile concentrations approach a plateau, but nonvolatile degradation products remain; steam stripping does not remove the entire deterioration burden.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Increased viscosity and persistent foaming
detailed_explanations.explanation: Coupled and polymerised lipid products increase average molecular size and viscosity. They contribute to gums, deposits, persistent foaming, darker oil and potentially greater oil retention by fried food.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Free fatty acids are more volatile and contribute to earlier smoking
detailed_explanations.explanation: Hydrolysis releases free fatty acids, increases acidity and contributes to smoking at lower temperatures. Smoke point also depends on refining history and other constituents, so free-fatty-acid content is not its sole determinant.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: It may rise and later fall as hydroperoxides decompose
detailed_explanations.explanation: The concentration of hydroperoxides reflects the balance between formation and decomposition. The handout explicitly notes an induction period followed by a rise and later fall. At frying temperatures decomposition can be rapid, so peroxide value alone is inadequate.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Oxidised polar compounds and polymerised glycerides
detailed_explanations.explanation: Frying generates nonpolymeric polar compounds such as hydroxyl and epoxy acids, as well as dimeric and polymeric acids and glycerides. Volatile aldehydes and ketones may partly escape with steam, but nonvolatile products remain.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Accumulation of degradation products, including polymers and polar compounds
detailed_explanations.explanation: Persistent chemical foaming must be distinguished from normal steam bubbles. Darkening, increased viscosity, gums and persistent foam are compatible with accumulated frying-oil degradation products. No single sensory observation substitutes for a complete assessment.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Lipid exchange from fatty foods such as chicken
detailed_explanations.explanation: Fatty foods can release endogenous lipids into the frying medium. This lipid exchange can change the frying oil's fatty-acid composition and oxidative stability.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: It does not adequately capture secondary oxidation, hydrolysis or polymerisation
detailed_explanations.explanation: Peroxide value measures primary peroxide-related oxidation. Hydroperoxides can decompose while secondary products, free fatty acids and polymers accumulate. A defensible evaluation combines process history, acidity, primary and secondary oxidation measures, polar products and the applicable verified legal criterion.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Neither figure is established by the supplied documents as a verified legal provision
detailed_explanations.explanation: The handout expressly states that neither uploaded document establishes the governing legal provision, exact applicability or boundary wording for 15% and 25% TPC. The figures must not be quoted as verified law from the fortification compendium.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Control time and temperature, remove food debris and assess oil using complementary measures
detailed_explanations.explanation: The handout recommends controlling time and temperature, removing food debris, minimising idle heating and repeated thermal cycling, assessing oil with suitable measurements, and applying the verified statutory discard criterion. Fresh-oil replenishment does not justify indefinite use.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Holoenzyme
detailed_explanations.explanation: The apoenzyme is the protein portion of a cofactor-dependent enzyme. When combined with its required nonprotein component (cofactor), it forms the holoenzyme, the complete catalytic system.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Pepsinogen → pepsin; trypsinogen → trypsin
detailed_explanations.explanation: Pepsinogen and trypsinogen are inactive precursors activated to pepsin and trypsin, commonly through limited proteolysis. A zymogen is not simply an apoenzyme missing a cofactor.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Hydrolases
detailed_explanations.explanation: Lipase catalyses hydrolysis of carboxylic ester bonds and is therefore a hydrolase (EC class 3). The handout gives EC number 3.1.1.3.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Lyases
detailed_explanations.explanation: Pectate lyase catalyses nonhydrolytic elimination reactions and belongs to the lyases. The handout flags the absolute claim that all pectin-degrading enzymes are hydrolases as incorrect.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Enzyme class
detailed_explanations.explanation: The first EC digit indicates the reaction class. The handout teaches the traditional six classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases and ligases. Modern EC classification also includes translocases as a seventh class.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: The handout presents the traditional six-class system; modern EC classification also recognises translocases
detailed_explanations.explanation: The source specifically teaches the traditional six-class system and cautions that modern Enzyme Commission classification also includes translocases. In a source-specific question asking for the handout's six classes, reproduce its six listed classes while avoiding the claim that the modern system has only six.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: The initial rate is half of Vmax
detailed_explanations.explanation: Substituting [S] = Km into v = Vmax[S]/(Km+[S]) gives v = Vmax/2. Km has concentration units. This interpretation applies to the relevant Michaelis–Menten model.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Vmax
detailed_explanations.explanation: When substrate concentration is much greater than Km, enzyme active sites are nearly saturated and v approaches Vmax. The rate becomes approximately zero order with respect to further increases in substrate.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Km is a kinetic constant and approaches Kd only under a limiting assumption
detailed_explanations.explanation: For the simple scheme, Km = (k−1 + kcat)/k1, while Kd = k−1/k1. Km approaches Kd when catalytic conversion is much slower than ES dissociation. It is not universally an equilibrium dissociation constant.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: 50 µmol/min
detailed_explanations.explanation: At [S] = Km, the rate is half-maximal. Therefore v = 100 × 2/(2+2) = 50 µmol/min. This is the defining half-maximum relationship.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: 1/Vmax
detailed_explanations.explanation: The double-reciprocal equation is 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax. Thus the slope is Km/Vmax, vertical intercept is 1/Vmax and horizontal intercept is −1/Km.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Apparent Km to increase while Vmax remains unchanged
detailed_explanations.explanation: Competitive inhibitor binds free enzyme in a manner mutually exclusive with substrate. Apparent Km increases, while Vmax remains unchanged; sufficiently high substrate can overcome the inhibition in the elementary model.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Unchanged Km and decreased Vmax
detailed_explanations.explanation: In pure noncompetitive inhibition, inhibitor binds free enzyme and enzyme–substrate complex with equal affinity. Vmax decreases while Km remains unchanged. Binding away from the active site alone does not establish pure noncompetitive kinetics.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Only enzyme–substrate complex
detailed_explanations.explanation: An uncompetitive inhibitor binds only the enzyme–substrate complex. In the classical model, both apparent Km and Vmax decrease by the same factor; increasing substrate does not restore the original maximum rate.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Increase or decrease depending on relative inhibitor binding
detailed_explanations.explanation: Mixed inhibitors bind both free enzyme and enzyme–substrate complex with unequal affinities. Apparent Vmax decreases, while apparent Km may increase or decrease depending on the relative binding constants.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Succinate dehydrogenase
detailed_explanations.explanation: The handout uses malonate as a competitive inhibitor in comparison with succinate at succinate dehydrogenase. The structural/functional substrate competition raises apparent Km without changing Vmax in the simple model.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Raises molecular collision frequency and reaction rate
detailed_explanations.explanation: Temperature initially increases molecular motion and collision frequency, often raising reaction rate. Beyond an enzyme-specific optimum, thermal unfolding and loss of active structure reduce activity. Enzymes do not change the equilibrium constant of the uncoupled reaction.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: It changes ionisation of catalytic groups and may disrupt structure
detailed_explanations.explanation: Hydrogen-ion concentration affects ionisation states of amino-acid side chains involved in binding and catalysis and can disrupt structural interactions. Each enzyme has a characteristic pH profile; extremes may denature or inactivate it.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Chymosin
detailed_explanations.explanation: Chymosin (rennin) acts on κ-casein and destabilises casein micelles, enabling coagulation during cheese manufacture. The handout references chymosin in the proteolysis/industrial enzyme context.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Catalase and peroxidase
detailed_explanations.explanation: Catalase and peroxidase are endogenous enzymes commonly considered in evaluating adequacy of blanching. Their residual activity can indicate insufficient heat treatment; the appropriate indicator depends on the commodity and process.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: An enzyme lowers the activation barrier but does not change the equilibrium position of the uncoupled reaction
detailed_explanations.explanation: Enzymes provide a lower-activation-energy pathway and increase the rate at which equilibrium is approached. They do not alter the equilibrium constant or make an uncoupled thermodynamically unfavourable reaction favourable by themselves.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Chlorophylls
detailed_explanations.explanation: Chlorophylls are the principal green pigments in green plant tissues. Their central magnesium and conjugated ring system contribute to visible light absorption.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Pheophytin
detailed_explanations.explanation: Acid and heat can displace the central magnesium ion of chlorophyll, producing pheophytin and an olive-brown colour. This is a common processing-related colour change.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Yellow, orange and red
detailed_explanations.explanation: Carotenoids are conjugated polyene pigments commonly responsible for yellow, orange and red colours. They are lipid-soluble and include carotenes and xanthophylls.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: C40 describes the parent carotenoid framework, but cleavage products such as bixin and norbixin are exceptions
detailed_explanations.explanation: The handout warns against treating C40 as an absolute rule for every related pigment. The parent carotenoid framework is commonly C40, while apocarotenoid cleavage products such as bixin and norbixin have fewer carbon atoms.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: pH
detailed_explanations.explanation: Anthocyanins undergo pH-dependent structural equilibria, producing different colour forms. Acidic conditions commonly favour red flavylium forms, while higher pH can shift hue and may promote instability.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Yellow or cream/white flavonoid pigments
detailed_explanations.explanation: Anthoxanthins are pale yellow, cream or white flavonoid pigments. Their colour can change with pH and metal interactions; they should not be confused with anthocyanins.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: They are nitrogen-containing pigments derived from tyrosine and betalamic acid
detailed_explanations.explanation: The handout corrects an older textbook label: modern chemical classification identifies betalains as nitrogen-containing pigments derived from tyrosine and betalamic acid, not chemically indigoid pigments.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Myoglobin
detailed_explanations.explanation: Myoglobin is the principal muscle pigment. Its colour depends on the chemical state of its heme iron and the ligands bound to it; oxygenation and oxidation state are central to meat colour.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Metmyoglobin
detailed_explanations.explanation: Oxidation of the heme iron to the ferric state produces metmyoglobin, associated with brown discoloration. Oxymyoglobin is associated with bright cherry-red colour, while deoxymyoglobin gives a purplish-red appearance.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Excessive heat, oxygen and unfavourable pH
detailed_explanations.explanation: Pigment stability depends on molecular structure and the food environment. Heat, oxygen, pH and light can accelerate degradation or shift pigment forms. The exact response is pigment-specific, so the option states a broad risk combination rather than a universal single pathway.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Tea polyphenols
detailed_explanations.explanation: Tea processing involves enzymatic oxidation of polyphenolic substrates, with quinone formation and subsequent condensation/polymerisation contributing to characteristic coloured products such as theaflavins and thearubigins.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Oxygen
detailed_explanations.explanation: PPO catalyses oxidation of phenolic substrates using molecular oxygen. Cutting or bruising tissue brings phenolics, active enzyme and oxygen together, producing quinones that subsequently form brown polymers.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Phenolic substrate → ortho-quinone → coupling/condensation products
detailed_explanations.explanation: In PPO-mediated browning, monophenols may first be hydroxylated to ortho-diphenols (monophenolase activity), then oxidised to ortho-quinones (diphenolase activity). Quinones undergo largely nonenzymatic coupling and condensation to melanin-like pigments.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Taste, aroma and other sensory inputs including mouthfeel
detailed_explanations.explanation: Flavour is a combined sensory experience. Taste and olfaction are central, while texture, mouthfeel, temperature and trigeminal sensations also influence perception.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Umami taste
detailed_explanations.explanation: MSG supplies glutamate, which stimulates umami taste receptors and enhances savoury character. It is a flavour enhancer rather than an intense sweetener.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Enhancement of sweet, caramel-like or cooked flavour notes
detailed_explanations.explanation: Maltol and ethyl maltol are flavour compounds used to enhance sweet, caramel-like and cooked notes. Their function is sensory enhancement, not pigment synthesis or protein hydrolysis.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Bulk sweeteners contribute appreciable mass, while intense sweeteners provide sweetness at much lower use levels
detailed_explanations.explanation: Bulk sweeteners contribute body and solids as well as sweetness, whereas intense sweeteners have much greater sweetness potency and are used at lower concentrations. Their metabolism and energy contribution differ by compound.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: It is an intense sweetener and is metabolised
detailed_explanations.explanation: Aspartame is an intense sweetener that is metabolised; the handout explicitly warns that intense sweetness does not imply that all sweeteners are excreted unchanged. It must not be grouped indiscriminately with non-metabolised compounds.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Replace some of the mass and functional solids of sugar
detailed_explanations.explanation: Bulk sweeteners can contribute solids, body, texture and sometimes humectancy, functions that an intense sweetener used in tiny quantities may not replace. Formulation often requires additional bulking agents or texture modifiers.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: They can intensify or modify existing savoury or characteristic flavour notes
detailed_explanations.explanation: Flavour enhancers modify or intensify sensory perception, often by strengthening existing flavour notes. They are not automatically preservatives or colourants and do not create every flavour characteristic from nothing.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Different intense sweeteners have different chemical structures, metabolism and exposure profiles
detailed_explanations.explanation: Sweetness potency is a sensory property, not a predictor of metabolism, toxicology or excretion. The handout uses aspartame as a specific warning against assuming all intense sweeteners pass through unchanged.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Aroma
detailed_explanations.explanation: Volatile molecules released from food reach olfactory receptors through the nasal route, contributing aroma. Flavour perception integrates this with taste and other oral sensory inputs.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Nature-identical synthetic colour
detailed_explanations.explanation: Nature-identical synthetic colours are chemically manufactured to reproduce a naturally occurring colour molecule. This differs from extraction of a natural pigment and from synthetic colours without a natural counterpart.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Annatto
detailed_explanations.explanation: Annatto is a natural colour source associated with carotenoid pigments such as bixin and norbixin. The other listed examples are synthetic colours.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Eight
detailed_explanations.explanation: The uploaded handout's section 7 explicitly treats eight synthetic colours listed in the textbook. This question tests the source-specific count, not a general claim about every current regulatory list.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: The accessible compendium separately permits titanium dioxide in double fortified salt; the handout also discusses a specific chewing-gum exception in its textbook section
detailed_explanations.explanation: The correction register warns that a colour prohibition must not be expanded into a ban on every inorganic additive. Schedule I separately permits titanium dioxide in double fortified salt. The textbook section discusses a specific chewing-gum exception; scope and governing provision must be kept distinct.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Converting a water-soluble dye into an insoluble pigment form on a suitable substrate
detailed_explanations.explanation: Lake colours are insoluble pigment preparations made by precipitating or adsorbing a soluble dye onto an appropriate substrate, commonly an aluminium-containing substrate. Their suitability depends on the food system and applicable permission.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: pH, heat exposure, light stability and food matrix
detailed_explanations.explanation: Colour stability depends on pigment chemistry and matrix conditions. pH, heat, oxygen, light, moisture and interactions with other ingredients can alter hue, intensity or stability; selection should reflect the product's processing and storage conditions.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Use the list as historical/source material and verify the current governing regulation before asserting legal permission
detailed_explanations.explanation: The handout's source audit distinguishes textbook information from statutory authority and warns against unsupported legal claims. A list in a textbook or 2021 compendium does not automatically verify current permission, category, maximum level or conditions.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Curcumin
detailed_explanations.explanation: Curcumin is the yellow pigment associated with turmeric. MSG is a savoury flavour enhancer, while maltol and ethyl maltol are flavour compounds.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Deliberately increasing essential micronutrients in food to improve nutritional quality and provide public-health benefit with minimal health risk
detailed_explanations.explanation: The handout reproduces the Regulation 2 definition: fortification is deliberate increase of essential micronutrients to improve nutritional quality and provide public-health benefit with minimal health risk. It is a controlled public-health intervention, not simply an appearance claim.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: A substance added to food to provide micronutrients, excluding the specified nutraceuticals and foods for Special Dietary Uses
detailed_explanations.explanation: The Regulation 2 definition in the compendium describes a fortificant as a substance added to food to provide micronutrients, excluding nutraceuticals and foods for Special Dietary Uses. The distinction is statutory and should be retained.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: The provisions set conditions for a product when it is fortified; the phrase alone does not mandate fortification of every product
detailed_explanations.explanation: The handout emphasises that 'when fortified' imposes conditions on fortified products but does not by itself make fortification universally compulsory for every product in the category. Mandatory fortification requires the public-health basis and direction described in Regulation 3.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Heme iron in any form
detailed_explanations.explanation: Regulation 3(4), as reproduced in the compendium, states that heme iron shall not be used in any form in any article of food. The other options appear as permitted iron sources in specified Schedule I vehicles, subject to the individual table.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: 15–30 ppm on dry-weight basis
detailed_explanations.explanation: The source-audited handout states that the August 2021 amendment substituted a 15–30 parts-per-million range on a dry-weight basis. It distinguishes the earlier two-stage provision of 20–30 ppm at manufacture and 15–30 ppm at distribution. The compendium records 27 August 2021 as in-force date and 1 March 2022 as compliance date.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: The rice table lists ferric pyrophosphate or sodium feredetate, while atta/maida tables include additional iron compounds
detailed_explanations.explanation: The handout explicitly warns not to transfer the complete atta iron-source list automatically to rice. The rice table lists ferric pyrophosphate or sodium feredetate, while atta and maida list additional compounds. Vehicle-specific table entries must be followed.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Iron, folic acid and vitamin B12
detailed_explanations.explanation: The Schedule I tables reproduced in the handout require iron, folic acid and vitamin B12 for fortified atta and maida. Optional additional micronutrients are separately listed and should not be confused with the core required combination.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: More than 50% wheat flour
detailed_explanations.explanation: The compendium states that multigrain atta may use fortified-atta levels if it contains more than 50% wheat flour. The literal 'more than' condition means exactly 50% does not satisfy the wording.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: The package may also carry the tagline; the fortification declaration and prescribed logo are otherwise required, subject to the stated iodized-salt exception
detailed_explanations.explanation: The handout flags a common trap: Regulation 7(2) says the package may also carry the tagline, making it optional. The words 'fortified with' followed by the fortificant name and prescribed logo are required, subject to the stated exception for iodized salt fortified with iodine.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: An exception limited to the requirements of Regulation 7(2)
detailed_explanations.explanation: The compendium limits the exception to Regulation 7(2) for iodized salt fortified with iodine. It is not a blanket exemption from food law, quality standards or all other labelling requirements; it should not automatically be extended to iron-containing double fortified salt.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: People with thalassemia may take under medical supervision, and persons with sickle cell anaemia are advised not to consume iron-fortified food products
detailed_explanations.explanation: The substituted advisory distinguishes two groups: people with thalassemia may take iron-fortified foods under medical supervision, while persons with sickle cell anaemia are advised not to consume them. The handout warns against replacing this with the earlier thalassemia-only wording.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: A guarantee that every fortified food cures micronutrient deficiency
detailed_explanations.explanation: Regulation 5 obligations in the compendium include a twice-yearly undertaking, notified-laboratory certification, records and inventory of fortificants, stage-wise monitoring, random testing, equipment/process audits and good manufacturing practices. A disease-cure guarantee is not a quality-assurance obligation and would be an unsupported therapeutic claim.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Minus 10% of the declared total value, while preserving the Schedule I maximum for added micronutrients
detailed_explanations.explanation: The handout states that the substituted Regulation 4(1) permits a tolerance of minus 10% of the declared total value for compliance and analysis, while preserving the Schedule I maximum for added micronutrients. It is not a general positive tolerance or permission to exceed the maximum.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Not recommended for direct consumption; only for named Government-funded programme; reconstitute the entire contents as directed; once opened, consume the same day
detailed_explanations.explanation: The August 2021 insertion described in the compendium restricts fortified milk powder to Government-funded programmes for preparing reconstituted fortified milk. The label must state it is not recommended for direct consumption, programme restriction, reconstitution of the entire contents as directed, and same-day consumption after opening.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: They may be added singly or in combination, but specified sources and levels still matter when used
detailed_explanations.explanation: The Schedule I section lists optional micronutrients that may be added singly or in combination. Optional status does not remove the obligation to use the prescribed source and level when the nutrient is added.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: The exclusion in the handout concerns the Fortified Processed Foods category
detailed_explanations.explanation: The correction register specifies that Regulation 3(7) excludes HFSS foods from the Fortified Processed Foods category. It should not be widened into a claim that HFSS foods are excluded from every possible meaning or provision concerning fortified food.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Not established by the accessible Schedule II extraction and therefore not to be invented
detailed_explanations.explanation: The source audit explicitly says the accessible Schedule II extraction does not establish numerical logo dimensions or Pantone 3005 C. These specifications should not be quoted as established by the supplied text without checking the authoritative complete instrument.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: In force 22 September 2021; compliance 1 April 2022
detailed_explanations.explanation: The handout distinguishes the amendment's in-force date (22 September 2021) from the compliance date (1 April 2022). The August 2021 amendments have a different timeline: in force 27 August 2021 and compliance 1 March 2022.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Compliance combines vehicle-specific nutrient levels and permitted sources with packaging, labelling, quality assurance and general food-law obligations
detailed_explanations.explanation: The handout frames fortification as a regulated public-health intervention. It links nutrient standards and permitted sources with packaging that protects nutrient retention, declarations and logo, specific advisories, quality assurance, records, testing and compliance with generally applicable food law.
